The animaos command line for scaffolding an agent workspace and running agents and swarms on the daemon

import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`animaos` is a thin command-line client of the Rust daemon. It does two kinds of work:

- local scaffolding of a single-agent workspace with `create`
- daemon-backed execution with `launch`, `run`, `chat`, `agents` and `assistant`

The daemon does the thinking; the CLI creates agents or swarms over HTTP, sends a task and prints the result. Most day-to-day use of anima happens in the web console, so treat the CLI as the scripting and terminal surface.

## Mental Model

- `animaos create` scaffolds a local single-agent workspace (`anima.yaml` plus profile files). It does not need the daemon.
- `animaos launch` runs an `anima.yaml` workspace as a swarm on the daemon. With no `--no-tui` it opens the [TUI](/tui/).
- `animaos run` sends one task to a temporary agent or swarm and prints plain text.
- `animaos chat` opens a plain-text REPL with a new daemon agent.
- `animaos agents` lists and shows the agents the daemon holds.
- `animaos assistant` chats with an existing agent by name (see the caution below).

## Installation

`@animaOS-SWARM/cli` is a private workspace package; it is not published to npm. Build it from the repository and run it through the root script:

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run build:cli-sdk
bun run animaos --help
```

`bun run animaos` runs `node packages/cli/dist/index.js`, the package's `animaos` binary. Examples on this site write `animaos ...`; in the repository, use `bun run animaos ...`.

<Aside type="note">
  `create` is local. `launch`, `run`, `chat`, `agents` and `assistant` talk to the daemon over HTTP, so a daemon must be running first (`bun run daemon`, or the installed `anima` program). The CLI sends no credentials, so it works against a daemon that has no `ANIMAOS_RS_API_KEY` set.
</Aside>

## In This Section

- [Agency Workflow](/cli/workspaces/) covers `create`, the `anima.yaml` format, seed memories, `launch` and history files.
- [Daemon Commands](/cli/daemon/) covers `run`, `chat`, `agents`, `assistant` and targeting a daemon.
- [Providers & Environment](/cli/providers/) covers provider names, credentials and environment variables.

## Fast Path

<Steps>

1. Start the daemon.

   ```bash
   bun run daemon
   ```

2. Scaffold an agent workspace.

   ```bash
   animaos create agent content-writer \
     -d "Research topics and write high-quality articles"
   ```

3. Launch that workspace in the TUI.

   ```bash
   cd content-writer
   animaos launch
   ```

</Steps>

## Command Guide

### `animaos create`

Scaffold a single-agent workspace directory. This is a local filesystem workflow.

```bash
# Interactive mode: prompts for the agent name and description
animaos create

# Single-agent workspace
animaos create agent medicine-helper \
  -d "Research medical literature and summarize risks clearly"
```

`create` makes no model call. It writes the workspace from a template and records the provider in `anima.yaml`: the one you pass with `-p`, otherwise the first remote provider that has credentials in your environment, otherwise `deterministic`. Multi-agent agencies are not generated; write `anima.yaml` by hand for those (see [Agency Workflow](/cli/workspaces/#animayaml)) and run them with `animaos launch`. `animaos create agency` is refused with that message.

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `--kind` | | `agent`; equivalent to `animaos create agent ...` |
| `-p, --provider` | auto | Provider recorded in the workspace (see [Providers](/cli/providers/)); an unknown name is an error |
| `-m, --model` | `gpt-4o-mini` | Model recorded in the workspace |
| `-d, --description` | | What the agent should do (prompted when omitted) |
| `--system` | | Custom system prompt for the agent |
| `--api-key` | | API key, used only to detect which provider is configured |

The directory name is the agent name, lowercased and kebab-cased. It contains:

```text
medicine-helper/
├── anima.yaml        # config used by launch
├── org-chart.mmd     # Mermaid org chart
├── README.md         # mission, values, roster
└── agents/
    └── medicine-helper/
        ├── profile.md
        ├── assets/
        └── memory/
```

### `animaos launch`

Run a workspace's `anima.yaml` as a swarm on the daemon.

```bash
cd content-team

animaos launch                                    # TUI, interactive
animaos launch "Write an article about Rust macros"   # TUI, one task
animaos launch --no-tui "Write an article about Rust macros"   # plain text, one task
animaos launch --no-tui                           # plain-text prompt
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `-d, --dir <dir>` | `.` | Directory containing `anima.yaml` |
| `--api-key <key>` | | API key for the agency's provider, for this run |
| `--no-tui` | | Plain text instead of the Ink TUI |

Without `anima.yaml` in the directory, `launch` fails with `No anima.yaml found ... Run "animaos create" first`. Before sending a task it checks `GET /health` and warns when the daemon is unreachable.

Plain-text interactive launch prompts with `task >` and supports:

| Input | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `exit` (or an empty line) | Quit |
| `/help` | Show the commands |
| `/health` | Recheck daemon connectivity |

### `animaos run`

Run a temporary agent, or a temporary swarm with `-s`, for one task.

```bash
# Single agent
animaos run "Summarize the Rust book" -m gpt-4o-mini

# Swarm with a manager and one worker
animaos run "Build a landing page" -s supervisor -m gpt-4o
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `-m, --model` | `gpt-4o-mini` | Model to use |
| `-p, --provider` | `openai` | Provider |
| `-n, --name` | `task-agent` | Agent name (single-agent mode) |
| `-s, --strategy` | | `supervisor`, `dynamic` or `round-robin`; switches to swarm mode |
| `--api-key` | | API key override |
| `--no-tui` | | Skips the "TUI not available" note; `run` is always plain text |

Output is the result, then `Duration: ...ms | Tokens: ...`. A failed task prints the error and exits with code 1. Each `run` registers a new agent (or swarm) in the daemon; it is not removed afterwards.

<Aside type="caution">
  `run` is always plain text. Without `--no-tui` it first prints a note that TUI mode is not available for daemon-backed runs, then continues in plain text; pass `--no-tui` to skip the note.
</Aside>

### `animaos chat`

```bash
animaos chat -m claude-sonnet-4-5 -p anthropic
```

Creates a daemon agent and opens a REPL with a `you >` prompt. Type `exit` (or an empty line) to quit. Options: `-p, --provider` (default `openai`), `-m, --model` (default `gpt-4o-mini`), `-n, --name` (default `task-agent`) and `--api-key`. Each message is a blocking `agents.run()` call, and the agent stays registered after you exit.

### `animaos agents`

```bash
animaos agents list                  # every agent the daemon holds
animaos agents show researcher       # by name or id
```

`list` prints each agent's name, id, status, model and message and event counts. `show` adds token usage and the last task's status.

### `animaos assistant`

```bash
animaos assistant                    # same as: animaos assistant chat
animaos assistant chat -n assistant --user-name "Sam"
```

`assistant chat` is a REPL against an agent that already exists on the daemon, found by name (`-n, --name`, default `assistant`). It sends your `userId` and `userName` in each message's metadata (`--user-id` and `--user-name`, falling back to `ANIMAOS_USER_ID`, `ANIMAOS_USER_NAME` and the operating-system user name).

<Aside type="caution">
  The command's error text and `animaos assistant inbox` refer to an assistant mode and an `/api/assistant/outbox` route that the current Rust daemon does not serve. Expect `inbox` to fail with an HTTP error. For ongoing conversations with your agents, use the web console or the [Sessions & Runs](/sdk/sessions/) API.
</Aside>

## Environment

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `ANIMA_DAEMON_URL` | Daemon base URL for every daemon-backed command. Default `http://127.0.0.1:8080`; an installed `anima` program serves on `http://127.0.0.1:8787` |
| Provider key and base-URL variables | Used to detect and forward credentials. See [Providers & Environment](/cli/providers/) |
| `ANIMAOS_USER_ID`, `ANIMAOS_USER_NAME` | Defaults for `assistant chat` |

The daemon has its own settings (port, workspace root, persistence) that the CLI does not read; see the [daemon README](https://github.com/G9000/animaOS-SWARM/blob/main/hosts/rust-daemon/README.md#environment-variables).

## Good Defaults

- Use `create` and `launch` for a durable, human-editable workspace and the TUI.
- Use `run` for a one-off answer.
- Use `chat` for a quick agent REPL without a workspace.
- Use `agents` to see what the daemon holds after runs and restarts.
Run, chat, inspect, and target the daemon from the CLI

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

These commands talk to the Rust daemon instead of writing local workspace files. Start a daemon first: `bun run daemon` from the repository, or the installed `anima` program.

## Choose the Right Command

| Command | Use it when | Notes |
|---------|-------------|-------|
| `run` | You want one result now | Creates a temporary agent (or swarm with `-s`) and prints plain text |
| `chat` | You want an interactive REPL with one agent | Creates one daemon agent and keeps the conversation open |
| `agents` | You want to inspect what the daemon holds | Lists and shows registered agents |
| `assistant` | You want to chat with an existing agent by name | Sends your user id and name as metadata |

## `animaos run`

```bash
# Single agent
animaos run "Summarize the Rust book" -m gpt-4o-mini

# Swarm
animaos run "Build a landing page" -s supervisor -m gpt-4o
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `-m, --model` | `gpt-4o-mini` | Model to use |
| `-p, --provider` | `openai` | Provider (see [Providers](/cli/providers/)) |
| `-n, --name` | `task-agent` | Agent name (single-agent mode) |
| `-s, --strategy` | | `supervisor`, `dynamic` or `round-robin` |
| `--api-key` | | API key override |
| `--no-tui` | | Skips the "TUI not available" note |

In single-agent mode `run` creates an agent with the system prompt `You are a helpful task agent. Use tools when needed. Be concise.` and runs your task. With `-s` it creates a swarm with a manager and one worker using the same model and provider, runs the task, and prints the swarm's result and token total. Credentials are forwarded with the request (`--api-key`, otherwise the provider's environment variables), so switching keys never needs a daemon restart.

The agent or swarm stays registered in the daemon after the command finishes. They appear in `animaos agents list`, and agents can be removed with the SDK's `client.agents.remove()`.

## `animaos chat`

```bash
animaos chat -m claude-sonnet-4-5 -p anthropic
```

`chat` creates a daemon agent and opens a terminal REPL at `you >`. Type `exit` or press Enter on an empty line to quit. Replies print as `agent > ...`; a failed run prints `[error] ...` and the prompt returns. Options match `run` except for `-s`: `-p`, `-m`, `-n` and `--api-key`.

## `animaos agents`

```bash
animaos agents list
animaos agents show researcher
```

`list` prints a count, then each agent's name, id, status, model and message and event counts, or `No daemon-backed agents are currently registered.` `show` accepts a name or an id and adds token usage and the last task status; an unknown name prints the available agents and exits with code 1. Use it to check daemon state after launches, retries or restarts.

## `animaos assistant`

```bash
animaos assistant chat --name assistant --user-id sam --user-name Sam
```

Looks up an agent with that exact name on the daemon (default `assistant`) and opens the same kind of REPL as `chat`, attaching `{ userId, userName }` metadata to each message. If no agent has that name it exits with an error.

<Aside type="caution">
  `animaos assistant inbox [--since <ms>] [--limit <n>]` requests `/api/assistant/outbox`, a route the current Rust daemon does not serve, and the not-found error text mentions `ANIMAOS_RS_ASSISTANT_ENABLED`, which the daemon no longer reads. Treat `inbox` as unavailable.
</Aside>

## Targeting a Different Daemon

The CLI defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Point it elsewhere with `ANIMA_DAEMON_URL`:

```bash
# An installed `anima` program
ANIMA_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787 animaos agents list

# Another local port or host
ANIMA_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8081 animaos agents list
```

The CLI sends no authorization headers. It cannot reach a daemon that sets `ANIMAOS_RS_API_KEY`, and it does not use the owner routes (sessions, approvals and so on). For those, use the [SDK](/sdk/client/#authentication) with a custom `fetch`.

Provider names, credentials, base URLs, and runtime environment for the CLI

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The CLI accepts the same provider names across `create`, `launch`, `run` and `chat`. `deterministic` is also accepted: it is a scripted, non-LLM provider built into the daemon for offline testing, and `create` falls back to it when no remote provider has credentials.

The CLI only detects and forwards credentials. The daemon makes the model calls, and it has its own sources of keys (its environment, keys saved in the web console, a ChatGPT subscription), so a key does not have to come from the CLI at all.

## Provider Matrix

| Provider | Accepted names | Key env vars | Base URL env var | Notes |
|----------|----------------|--------------|------------------|-------|
| OpenAI | `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_KEY`, `OPENAI_TOKEN` | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | Native chat completions |
| Anthropic | `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_TOKEN`, `CLAUDE_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | Native Messages API |
| Google Gemini | `google`, `gemini` | `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_KEY`, `GOOGLE_AI_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_API_KEY` | `GOOGLE_BASE_URL` | Native `generateContent` |
| Ollama | `ollama` | `OLLAMA_API_KEY` (optional) | `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` | Local; OpenAI-compatible; no key required |
| Groq | `groq` | `GROQ_API_KEY`, `GROQ_KEY`, `GROQ_TOKEN` | `GROQ_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| xAI | `xai`, `grok` | `XAI_API_KEY`, `XAI_KEY`, `GROK_API_KEY` | `XAI_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| OpenRouter | `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_TOKEN` | `OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| Mistral | `mistral` | `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_KEY`, `MISTRAL_TOKEN` | `MISTRAL_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| Together | `together` | `TOGETHER_API_KEY`, `TOGETHER_KEY`, `TOGETHER_TOKEN` | `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| DeepSeek | `deepseek` | `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` | `DEEPSEEK_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| Fireworks | `fireworks` | `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` | `FIREWORKS_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| Perplexity | `perplexity` | `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` | `PERPLEXITY_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible |
| Moonshot | `moonshot`, `kimi` | `MOONSHOT_API_KEY`, `MOONSHOT_KEY`, `MOONSHOT_TOKEN`, `KIMI_API_KEY` | `MOONSHOT_BASE_URL`, `KIMI_BASE_URL` | OpenAI-compatible Moonshot/Kimi endpoint |

When several variables are listed, the CLI uses the first one that is set and non-empty. Default endpoints are each provider's public API (for example `https://api.openai.com/v1`, and `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` for Ollama).

## Runtime Environment

| Variable | Read by | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `ANIMA_DAEMON_URL` | CLI | Daemon base URL for daemon-backed commands (default `http://127.0.0.1:8080`) |
| Provider key variables | CLI and daemon | Forwarded by the CLI on each request; also read by the daemon itself |
| Provider base-URL variables | CLI and daemon | Override provider endpoints such as `OPENAI_BASE_URL` or `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` |
| `ANIMAOS_WORKSPACE_ROOT` | Daemon | Initial workspace root for the daemon's file tools (a configured workspace replaces it) |
| `ANIMAOS_USER_ID`, `ANIMAOS_USER_NAME` | CLI | Defaults for `animaos assistant chat` |

## Override Rules

- `--api-key` overrides the environment for one CLI invocation.
- For `launch`, `--api-key` applies to the agency's provider only; an agent that sets a different `provider` in `anima.yaml` uses that provider's own environment variables or credentials stored by the daemon.
- `create` falls back to `deterministic` when no remote provider is configured, and uses `--api-key` only to detect which provider is set up.
- Daemon-backed commands forward the resolved key and base URL as the agent's `settings.apiKey` and `settings.baseUrl`, so changing keys does not need a daemon restart.

## Common Examples

```bash
# Local Ollama
OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 \
animaos run "Summarize the plan" -p ollama -m qwen2.5:7b

# A daemon on another port
ANIMA_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787 \
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... \
animaos agents list

# Offline scaffolding with the deterministic provider
animaos create agent local-helper -d "Summarize notes" -p deterministic
```

<Aside type="tip">
  Keep provider credentials in the environment, use `--api-key` only for a temporary override, and use `ANIMA_DAEMON_URL` only when you intentionally target a different daemon. Credentials you connect in the web console (Settings, Model) are stored by the daemon and need no CLI flag at all.
</Aside>

This page covers the workflow that starts on disk: scaffold an agent workspace (or hand-write an `anima.yaml`), edit it like project files, then launch it on the daemon.

## Core Split

- `animaos create` is local. It writes files and does not need the daemon.
- `animaos launch` is daemon-backed. It reads `anima.yaml`, creates a swarm on the daemon (an orchestrator as manager, the `agents` as workers), and runs tasks through it.

## Create a Workspace

```bash
# Interactive prompt for name and description
animaos create

# Single-agent workspace
animaos create agent medicine-helper \
  -d "Research medical literature and summarize risks clearly"
```

`create` makes no model call. See the [CLI overview](/cli/#animaos-create) for its flags. It only scaffolds a single agent; for a multi-agent team, write `anima.yaml` yourself.

## Workspace Shape

```text
medicine-helper/
├── anima.yaml
├── org-chart.mmd
├── README.md
└── agents/
    └── medicine-helper/
        ├── profile.md
        ├── assets/
        └── memory/
```

- `anima.yaml` is the runtime config `launch` reads.
- `agents/<slug>/profile.md` is a human-readable profile. The slug is the agent name lowercased and kebab-cased.
- `agents/<slug>/memory/seed.json` holds optional starting memories. Add it by hand; `create` does not generate it.
- `org-chart.mmd` and `README.md` are generated documentation; `launch` does not read them.

## `anima.yaml`

```yaml
name: content-team
description: Researches topics and writes articles
model: gpt-4o-mini
provider: openai
strategy: supervisor
maxParallelDelegations: 2
orchestrator:
  name: editor
  bio: Senior editor who plans and reviews the work
  system: Break the task into steps, delegate to the team, and combine the results.
  tools: [memory_search, web_fetch]
agents:
  - name: researcher
    bio: Finds and checks facts
    system: Research the assigned topic and return concise findings.
    tools: [web_fetch, exa_search]
  - name: writer
    bio: Writes clear articles
    system: Turn findings into a polished article.
    model: gpt-4o
```

| Top-level key | Required | Default | Description |
|---------------|----------|---------|-------------|
| `name` | yes | | Agency name |
| `orchestrator` | yes | | The manager agent; needs `name`, `bio` and `system` |
| `agents` | no | `[]` | Worker agents |
| `description` | no | empty | Free text |
| `model` | no | `gpt-4o` | Default model for every agent |
| `provider` | no | `openai` | Default provider (see [Providers](/cli/providers/)) |
| `strategy` | no | `supervisor` | `supervisor`, `dynamic` or `round-robin` |
| `maxParallelDelegations` | no | | Passed to the swarm when set to a non-zero number |

Each agent (orchestrator or worker) accepts `name`, `bio`, `system`, `lore`, `adjectives`, `topics`, `knowledge`, `style`, `model` (overrides the agency model), `provider` (overrides the agency provider) and `tools`. A missing `name` becomes `unnamed`; names matter because seed memories are matched to agents by name.

`create` also writes `mission`, `values`, `position`, `role` and `collaboratesWith`, which feed the generated README and org chart. `launch` does not read them, so saving changes from the TUI's `/agents` panel rewrites `anima.yaml` without them.

### Tools

`tools` lists daemon tool names. Launch always gives every agent `memory_search` and `recent_memories` plus the memory plugin, and adds any of these you name: `memory_add`, `web_fetch`, `exa_search`, `get_current_time`, `calculate`, `read_file`, `list_dir`, `glob`, `grep`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, `multi_edit`, `todo_write`, `todo_read`, `bash`, `bg_start`, `bg_output`, `bg_stop` and `bg_list` (`memory_recent` is accepted as an alias of `recent_memories`). Any other entry is ignored with a warning, so unknown names stay declarative. Naming a tool only requests it: the daemon's own checks and the tool's prerequisites (for example a configured workspace for file tools) still apply.

## Launch a Workspace

```bash
cd medicine-helper

animaos launch                          # TUI, interactive
animaos launch "Summarize the latest research"   # TUI, one task
animaos launch --no-tui "Summarize the latest research"   # plain text
```

See the [CLI overview](/cli/#animaos-launch) for flags (`-d, --dir`, `--api-key`, `--no-tui`).

How launch builds the swarm:

- The orchestrator becomes the swarm manager and each entry in `agents` becomes a worker.
- Each agent's model is its own `model`, otherwise the agency `model`; its provider is its own `provider`, otherwise the agency `provider`.
- `--api-key` applies to the agency provider only. Provider credentials are otherwise taken from your environment.
- The swarm is created on the first task and reused for the session. After an error, or after you save an agent in the TUI, the next task builds a fresh swarm.

<Aside type="tip">
  Use `launch` when you care about a durable workspace, team composition, saved history or the TUI. Use [`run`](/cli/daemon/) for a one-off result without a workspace.
</Aside>

## Seed Memories

If an agent has `agents/<slug>/memory/seed.json`, `launch` posts those memories to the daemon after it creates the swarm, so the team starts with a baseline. The file is a JSON array (or a single object) of entries:

```json
[
  { "type": "fact", "content": "The audience is senior engineers.", "importance": 0.9, "tags": ["audience"] },
  { "type": "observation", "content": "Past articles ran about 800 words." }
]
```

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `type` | yes | `fact`, `observation`, `task_result` or `reflection` |
| `content` | yes | Non-empty text |
| `importance` | no | Number from 0 to 1 (default `0.5`) |
| `tags` | no | Array of strings |

Invalid files stop the launch with an error naming the agent and entry. Posting failures, or an agent name that is not in the swarm, are reported as warnings and never block the launch. On success the CLI prints `Seeded N memories from agents/<slug>/memory/seed.json`.

## Saved History

Every task `launch` runs (TUI or plain text) is appended to `anima-history.json` in the workspace directory, keeping the newest 100 entries. In the TUI the same file backs `/history` and `/resume`, and `/clear` empties it. TUI runs also write the latest task and result to `anima-result.md`. See [History & Resume](/tui/history/).

Recover work, ask questions, learn procedures, and automate native tools

## Continue interrupted work

An interrupted or failed owner task offers **Review interrupted work** below its recorded actions. Inspect those actions, especially any unknown outcome, acknowledge the review, then choose **Continue remaining work**. Anima starts a linked attempt in the same chat using current permissions and the original attachments and skill selection. It checks saved progress before acting; the original run and its action evidence stay available.

Repeated clicks return the same saved continuation, including after restart. Each chain allows at most three continuations. Work that was explicitly stopped, connector tasks, helpers and background jobs use their existing controls instead. Ordinary run-history retention still applies; unanswered questions keep their source available for recovery.

If a send or other external effect is uncertain, check the destination before authorizing continuation. A successful tool receipt alone cannot establish that the entire task succeeded. Anima never automatically replays an interrupted task.

## Ask while Anima works

Use `/btw <question>` in an existing web chat, or type it and choose **Ask side question**. The answer appears separately while the main task continues. It uses a bounded snapshot of the conversation, the active owner request and recorded progress; it does not use tools, change the main task or add a new task to its queue. The snapshot can be incomplete, and the side answer is not saved into the main transcript.

## Answer a question from Anima

Anima can show a question card with choices, multiple selections where requested, and a free-text answer. Choose **Submit answers** to save your response and let the waiting task continue. Answering grants no additional tool permissions.

Pending questions survive daemon restart. Submit the saved answers, then use the interrupted task's recovery review to continue; saving an answer after restart does not replay the old task. Owner stop cancels pending questions. Structured question cards are currently supported in ordinary web chats; connector and helper runs cannot open an unanswerable card.

## Completion and loop protection

Anima reviews settled file reads, checks and saved tasks before finishing. Repeated identical failures eventually lead to a final explanation with tools disabled. Repeated successful polling remains possible. Long runaway text is cut off and marked incomplete; text streamed before detection can remain visible. These checks help expose unfinished work; they are not a proof that every requested outcome is correct.

## Existing workspace data

The new durable state format is version 23. On first upgrade, the daemon preserves the exact version-22 file as `.pre-companion-interaction.bak`; older backups remain separate. No reset or data deletion is needed. Keep your configured persistent store and workspace path across restart.

## Learn a reusable procedure

Send `/learn <workflow or source>` in a chat. Include every source and constraint, for example:

```text
/learn docs/deployment.md and the workflow we just finished. Focus on rollback; skip production credentials.
```

Bare `/learn` uses the current conversation. This starts an ordinary task with the agent's current file, web and skill permissions. It gathers the sources and uses `propose_skill`; Strict and Custom leave a draft for review, while Free can activate it through the existing skill controls and keep an undo entry. The chat and Skills page show the actual result. Skills currently use one bounded `SKILL.md`; a multi-file book or document ingestion engine is not included.

## React to an event

Choose **Run when an event arrives** in the automation editor, or create a trigger through an already owner-authorized SDK client:

```ts
const automation = await client.automations.create(agentId, {
  name: 'Review changed files',
  prompt:
    'Review the changed file in the event payload and explain what needs attention.',
  trigger: { type: 'event', topic: 'files.changed' },
});

await client.automations.emitEvent(agentId, {
  eventId: 'file-revision-42',
  topic: 'files.changed',
  payload: { path: 'notes.txt' },
});
```

The owner endpoint is `POST /api/agents/{agentId}/automation-events`. It uses the same local owner authorization as automation changes: an approved local browser origin, or the configured local admin bearer token for a local adapter. It does not expose a public unauthenticated webhook. A file-change or webhook adapter can publish through this endpoint; Anima does not start a filesystem watcher.

Committed ordinary task outcomes, including reviewed recovery attempts, publish `task.completed` and `task.failed` for the task's agent. Pre-admission and start refusals, interrupted or cancelled work, schedules, helpers and other system followups do not publish these events. This prevents an automation from triggering itself through its own completion. Event payloads are source data; they do not grant tools, permissions or instructions. Existing active hours, approval rules, delivery targets and run history apply. Companion-created event automations run at least five minutes apart.

Reuse an `eventId` for retries of the same event. A different payload under a retained ID returns `409`. The daemon saves accepted occurrences before execution and retains their identities for the lifetime of the schedule. It admits at most 64 pending occurrences and 256 retained occurrences across live automations; new events return `429` when capacity is full, while exact retries remain duplicates. Deleting an automation releases its retained identities. Payloads must be JSON objects of at most 8 KiB, with bounded nesting. Native outcomes that cannot fit are logged and do not fail the original task. An interrupted claimed occurrence requires review and is not automatically replayed after restart.

## Chain native tools in a Python program

On Windows, explicitly select an installed Python 3.10 or newer interpreter before starting the daemon. Set `ANIMAOS_RS_TOOL_RPC_PYTHON_PATH` to its absolute executable path in that launch environment; restart the daemon after changing it. Anima does not discover an interpreter from personal profiles or install one automatically.

In the agent's access settings, choose shell access and enable **Allow programmatic tool chains**. This separately grants `execute_code`; each native tool also needs its own grant. The settings show whether the interpreter is configured. Configuration is not an execution health check.

The agent can then send a complete Python program to `execute_code`:

```python
from anima_tools import read_file, write_file

first = read_file(file_path="first.txt")
second = read_file(file_path="second.txt")
write_file(file_path="combined.txt", content=first + "\n" + second)
print("combined.txt was written")
```

Each call starts fresh; variables do not persist between programs. The generated `anima_tools` module includes only the currently granted subset of `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `glob`, `grep`, `edit_file`, `multi_edit` and `bash`. Native keyword arguments are unchanged. The outer program requires execution approval, and native calls keep their own approvals and durable receipts. Local Python has the operating-system access of the daemon user. Cancellation, a five-minute deadline and owned process cleanup remain enforced; uncertain effects require review.

import { Card, CardGrid, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**animaOS** is an agentic operating system: persistent AI agents, memory, tools and automations in one personal workspace. It runs on your computer or your own server, on top of your existing operating system. You choose the models, connect the tools, and decide how independently your agents work.

You talk to your agent (anima) in the web console or through a connected chat app. You give it work, let it bring in helpers, and follow its plans, actions and results in one place. Its context carries across conversations through saved memory and reusable skills.

This site documents the developer surfaces: the **TypeScript SDK**, the **`animaos` CLI** and the **terminal UI**. All three are thin clients of one process, the **Rust daemon**, which owns agents, memory, schedules, connectors and execution.

## What you can do with it

## Architecture

```text
 web console   SDK (TypeScript)   CLI (animaos)   TUI (animaos launch)   Telegram / Discord
      \              |                 |                  |                    /
       \_____________|_________________|__________________|___________________/
                                       |  HTTP + SSE
                         +-------------v--------------+
                         |   Rust daemon (anima-daemon)|   :8080 in development
                         |   Axum host, owner auth,    |   :8787 when installed
                         |   connectors, persistence   |
                         +-------------+--------------+
                                       |
        anima-core | anima-memory | anima-swarm | anima-schedule | anima-harness
                                       |
                              model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic,
                              Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, and more)
```

The reusable runtime lives in the Rust workspace under `packages/core-rust` and stays independent of any host. The daemon (`hosts/rust-daemon`) wraps it and exposes HTTP and server-sent events. The SDK, CLI and TUI never run agent code themselves; they call the daemon.

<Aside type="note">
  The Rust daemon is the only supported host today. Earlier TypeScript runtime packages, the mod system and the agency generator have been removed. `animaos create` scaffolds a single agent workspace, and `bun dev --host` accepts only `rust`.
</Aside>

## Ways to run it

| | Packaged `anima` | From the repository |
|---|------------------|---------------------|
| What it is | An installable program that wraps the daemon, embeds the web console, and adds a tray icon, supervisor and self-updater | The development workflow |
| Start | `anima setup`, then `anima` | `bun dev --host rust` |
| API and console | Port `8787` (control port `8788`) | Daemon on `8080`, web console on `4200` |
| Data | `~/.animaos-swarm/` | Its own development data |

The packaged program's commands include `anima`, `anima setup`, `anima status`, `anima start`, `anima stop`, `anima restart`, `anima quit`, `anima logs`, `anima update` and `anima config`. It is a separate copy from a development daemon; the two never share data or credentials. See the [packaged Anima guide](https://github.com/G9000/animaOS-SWARM/blob/main/apps/contributor-docs/src/content/docs/packaged-anima.md) for install, updates and limits.

For development, run from the repository root:

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun x nx run @animaOS-SWARM/sdk:build
bun dev --host rust
```

Then open `http://localhost:4200`, create your companion, select its workspace and connect a model provider. `bun run daemon` starts the daemon alone.

## Key concepts

### Agents

An agent is a persistent runtime registered with the daemon: a model and provider, a system prompt and character fields, tools, settings, memory, and a main conversation. You grant tools per agent, and an approval policy gates what they can do.

[Learn more about Agents](/sdk/agents/)

### Sessions and runs

Conversations are **sessions**. Sending a message creates a **run** that executes in the background; you follow it on a live event stream, and can steer or stop it. This is the model the web console uses.

[Learn more about Sessions & Runs](/sdk/sessions/)

### Swarms

A swarm is a manager and workers coordinated by a strategy: `supervisor`, `round-robin` or `dynamic`. The daemon streams their messages, tool calls and token usage.

[Learn more about Swarms](/sdk/swarms/)

### Memory

Agents keep facts, observations, task results and reflections, plus two always-on core blocks (About you and Agent notes). Retrieval fuses keyword matching, embeddings, relationships, temporal facts, recency and importance. Memory can be exported as JSON or Markdown.

[Learn more about Memories](/sdk/memories/)

### Approvals, jobs and automations

Tool calls are classed as read, write, exec, network or delegate; by default only exec asks. Jobs and automations let agents work without a chat message, and an unattended run that needs a decision waits for the owner.

[Learn more about Approvals](/sdk/approvals/) and [Jobs & Automations](/sdk/automations/)

### Persistence and durability

By default the daemon runs ephemeral. Configure a control-plane file (or Postgres), history and a memory store to keep agents, conversations and memories across restarts; the packaged program does this for you. A restart marks interrupted runs for review instead of replaying them.

Review tool calls that wait on the owner, set an agent's approval policy, and manage always-allow rules

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

An agent's tool calls are judged by its **approval policy** before they run. A call the policy sends to the owner waits as an **approval**, and its run shows `awaiting_approval` until you decide. This is how the web console's Needs-you inbox works, and `client.approvals` exposes the same operations.

<Aside type="caution">
  Every approval route is an owner route: scripts need `Authorization: Bearer <ANIMA_LOCAL_ADMIN_TOKEN>` (see [Authentication](/sdk/client/#authentication)). Decide approvals only from an owner-facing surface, never from an agent's own tool allowlist.
</Aside>

## Policy

Tools belong to a risk class. `read` tools never ask. The policy sets an action for the other four classes:

| Class | Covers | Default |
|-------|--------|---------|
| `write` | Changing files and saved state | `allow` |
| `exec` | Running commands and background processes | `ask` |
| `network` | Outbound requests | `allow` |
| `delegate` | Bringing in helpers or other agents | `allow` |

Each action is `allow`, `ask` or `deny`. The SDK exports `DEFAULT_APPROVAL_POLICY` and `POLICY_CLASSES`.

```typescript
const policy = await client.approvals.policy(agentId);

await client.approvals.setPolicy(agentId, { ...policy, exec: 'ask', network: 'ask' });
```

`setPolicy()` replaces the whole policy (all four classes) and returns it; it answers `409` for a helper, whose policy is its companion's. The console's per-agent autonomy modes (Free, Strict, Custom) sit on top of this policy and are set through `GET` and `PUT /api/agents/{agent_id}/autonomy`, which the SDK has no helper for (use `client.requestJson`); editing the class policy directly gives a Custom mode. Blocked commands and protected-action checks apply regardless.

## Review and Decide

```typescript
const { approvals } = await client.approvals.list({ status: 'pending', agentId });

for (const approval of approvals) {
  console.log(approval.tool, approval.class, approval.arguments, approval.expiresAtMs);
}

const decided = await client.approvals.decide(approvals[0].id, {
  decision: 'allow_once',
  revision: approvals[0].revision,
});
```

`list({ status, agentId?, cursor?, limit? })` returns `{ approvals, nextCursor }`. `pending` lists approvals waiting for the owner, oldest first. `decided` lists approvals from the last 30 days that were since decided, newest first, paged with `cursor` and `limit` (1 to 100, default 50).

An `Approval` carries `tool`, `class`, `arguments` (the call's arguments as JSON text, at most 16 KiB, with `argumentsTruncated`), `suggestedMatcher`, `matcherKinds`, `createdAtMs`, `expiresAtMs`, `status` (`pending`, `allowed`, `denied`, `stopped` or `expired`), `revision` and `resolution`. The model wrote the arguments, so show them as text, never as markup.

| `decision` | Effect |
|------------|--------|
| `allow_once` | Let this call run |
| `allow_session` | Also allow matching calls for the rest of the session (at most 50 allowances per session) |
| `allow_always` | Create a rule that allows matching calls (at most 100 rules per agent) |
| `deny` | Refuse; the model is told `Denied by owner: <note>` |

`decide(approvalId, { decision, revision, note?, matcher? })` needs the `revision` you read; a stale one is a `409` (`This approval changed; reload it and decide again`). `note` is at most `MAX_APPROVAL_NOTE_CHARS` (1,000) characters, and a denial's note reaches the model. `matcher` (`{ kind, value }`) applies to `allow_session` and `allow_always`; the approval's `suggestedMatcher` is used when it is absent. Repeating the same decision returns the approval unchanged, and deciding one already resolved another way (timeout, Stop or restart) is a `409`.

### Timing

A call that needs the owner waits up to 30 minutes (15 for a run started from Telegram). A timeout settles it as a denial noted `Approval timed out`. A daemon restart expires every pending approval. Helpers never wait: a call that would ask is denied. The `approval.requested` and `approval.resolved` [events](/sdk/sessions/#stream) announce changes; `isApprovalEvent()` narrows them.

<Aside type="note">
  Runs that nobody is watching also wait. With the default `exec: ask`, check-ins, jobs, Telegram and API runs that call `bash` wait for a decision, holding that automation or chat. For unattended shell work, set that agent's `exec` to `allow` or add a narrow rule.
</Aside>

## Rules

Rules are standing allowances for one tool.

```typescript
const { rules, tools } = await client.approvals.rules(agentId);

const rule = await client.approvals.addRule(agentId, {
  tool: 'bash',
  matcher: { kind: 'command_prefix', value: 'git status' },
});

await client.approvals.removeRule(agentId, rule.id);
```

`rules()` returns the agent's rules (oldest first) and every tool a rule can cover with its `class` and `matcherKinds`. Matcher kinds are `command_prefix`, `path_glob`, `domain` and `any` (an empty `value`). A command-prefix rule never covers a command containing a shell operator, and a path rule never covers an absolute path or one with `..`.

<Aside type="caution">
  Keep `exec` rules narrow. A rule for a shell, interpreter, HTTP client, package runner or `git`, or an `any` exec rule, lets the agent act as you on this machine, including through the loopback API. Workspace writes are allowed by default, so a file the agent can edit (`.git/config`, `package.json`) can turn a "safe" prefix rule into arbitrary code.
</Aside>

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Three SDK areas run work without you sending a chat message. All of them are owner routes, so scripts need `Authorization: Bearer <ANIMA_LOCAL_ADMIN_TOKEN>` (see [Authentication](/sdk/client/#authentication)), and they run inside the daemon, so the daemon must stay running for the work to continue.

| Area | Accessor | What it is |
|------|----------|------------|
| Jobs | `client.agents.jobs()` and related methods | A one-off prompt queued for an agent, with attempts and review |
| Goals | `client.goals` | A bounded objective that groups jobs under an attempt budget |
| Automations | `client.automations` | A prompt the daemon sends an agent on a trigger |

## Jobs

```typescript
const job = await client.agents.createJob(agentId, {
  title: 'Summarize open issues',
  prompt: 'Read the issue tracker export in the workspace and summarize the top five problems.',
  requestKey: 'issues-summary-2026-10-20',
  maxAttempts: 2,
  requiresApproval: true,
});

console.log(job.id, job.status); // 'awaiting_approval'

await client.agents.approveJob(agentId, job.id, { revision: job.revision });
```

`createJob(agentId, input)` explicitly queues execution. Durable jobs need daemon control-plane persistence (`ANIMAOS_RS_CONTROL_PLANE_FILE` or Postgres); without it the daemon answers `409`. Admission is refused while the daemon drains.

| `AgentJobInput` field | Description |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| `title` | Required, up to 160 characters |
| `prompt` | Required, up to 32 KiB |
| `requestKey` | Required, up to 128 bytes. Retain it when retrying an uncertain create with identical input |
| `maxAttempts` | 1 to 3 (default 3) |
| `requiresApproval` | Hold the job in `awaiting_approval` until the owner approves it |
| `goalId` | Attach the job to a goal |

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `jobs(agentId)` | List the agent's jobs |
| `createJob(agentId, input)` | Create and queue a job |
| `approveJob(agentId, jobId, { revision })` | Release a job waiting for approval |
| `cancelJob(agentId, jobId, { revision })` | Cancel a job |
| `retryJob(agentId, jobId, { revision, acknowledgeUncertain })` | Retry a failed, uncertain or changes-requested job below its attempt limit |
| `reviewJob(agentId, jobId, { revision, decision, note?, ... })` | Accept a result or request changes (`accepted` or `changes_requested`) |

Every mutation takes the job's current `revision`; a stale one is rejected. Statuses are `awaiting_approval`, `queued`, `running`, `pending_delegations` (waiting on helpers), `completed`, `failed`, `needs_review` and `cancelled`. A job has `attempt`, `maxAttempts`, an `attempts` history with each attempt's `result`, `error` and `review`, and `pendingDelegations` or `finalOutput` when helpers were involved.

A stopped or restart-interrupted attempt becomes `needs_review` because effects may already have happened. Retrying one requires `acknowledgeUncertain: true`. When you review a delegated final output, send `finalOutputGeneration` and `finalOutputSha256` from the job together.

The daemon keeps at most 200 jobs, runs at most 8 at once, and shares the global run limit.

## Goals

```typescript
const goal = await client.goals.create({
  title: 'Weekly report',
  objective: 'Produce a weekly summary of merged pull requests.',
  requestKey: 'weekly-report-v1',
  maxAttempts: 6,
});

const jobs = await client.goals.jobs(goal.id);
await client.goals.setStatus(goal.id, { revision: goal.revision, status: 'paused' });
```

A goal has a title (up to 160 characters), an objective (up to 32 KiB) and a `maxAttempts` budget of 1 to 100 shared by its jobs. A `GoalView` reports `status` (`active`, `paused` or `completed`), `consumedAttempts`, `reservedAttempts`, `remainingAttempts`, `jobCount` and `acceptedOutputs`. Methods: `list()`, `create(input)`, `setStatus(id, { revision, status })` and `jobs(id)`. The daemon keeps at most 50 goals.

## Automations

An automation is a prompt the daemon sends its agent on a trigger. Each one runs in its own thread unless it targets a connector.

```typescript
const automation = await client.automations.create(agentId, {
  name: 'Morning digest',
  prompt: 'Summarize anything that needs my attention today.',
  trigger: { type: 'daily', hour: 8, minute: 30, timeZone: 'Europe/Berlin' },
  activeHours: { start: '07:00', end: '22:00', days: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], timeZone: 'Europe/Berlin' },
});

console.log(automation.id, new Date(automation.nextDueAtMs));
```

### Triggers

| `trigger.type` | Fields | Notes |
|----------------|--------|-------|
| `interval` | `intervalMs` | Whole seconds |
| `daily` | `hour`, `minute`, `timeZone` | Wall-clock time in an IANA zone |
| `cron` | `expression`, `timeZone` | Five fields, or `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@midnight`, `@weekly`, `@monthly`, `@yearly`, `@annually`; `L`, `W`, `#` and `?` are refused |
| `once` | `atMs` | Fires once, then turns itself off |

A time a daylight-saving jump skips does not fire that day, and a repeated time fires once. `activeHours` (`start` and `end` as `HH:MM`, `days` as 0 for Sunday to 6, `timeZone`) keeps fires inside a window; an `end` before `start` runs overnight, and a `once` automation takes none. `target` is `{ type: 'workspace' }` (the default, its own thread) or `{ type: 'connector', connectorId }`.

### Methods

| Method | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| `list(agentId)` | Oldest first |
| `create(agentId, input)` | `prompt` and `trigger` required; `name` (1 to 80 characters, taken from the prompt when absent), `target`, `activeHours` and `enabled` optional |
| `createHeartbeat(agentId, { timeZone, prompt?, name?, target? })` | The heartbeat preset: every 30 minutes from 08:00 to 22:00 in `timeZone`. Any other field replaces the preset's |
| `update(agentId, id, patch)` | `prompt`, `trigger`, `target`, `enabled`, `name`; `activeHours: null` clears them. Turning a past `once` automation back on needs a new `atMs` |
| `remove(agentId, id)` | Delete. Fire records stay until the agent is deleted |
| `runNow(agentId, id)` | Fire it now; its due time and switch stay, and the occurrence is recorded as manual |
| `history(agentId, id, { limit? })` | Latest occurrences, newest first, at most 50 |
| `preview({ trigger, activeHours? })` | The next fire times the daemon computes: three, or one for `once` |

An `Automation` reports `enabled`, `nextDueAtMs`, `lastFiredAtMs`, `lastOutcome`, `running`, `counters` (`runs`, `failures`, `consecutiveFailures`), `createdBy` (the owner, or an agent's tool call) and `preset`. A history entry has an `outcome` of `silent`, `spoke`, `failed` or `stopped`. The SDK exports the limits `MAX_AUTOMATIONS_PER_AGENT` (20), `MAX_AUTOMATION_HISTORY` (50), `MAX_AUTOMATION_NAME_CHARS` (80) and `AUTOMATION_PREVIEW_RUNS` (3).

```typescript
const nextRuns = await client.automations.preview({
```

Create, search, recall, and manage agent memories with the animaOS SDK

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The daemon's memory system gives agents long-term recall. Memories are stored per agent, can be scoped to rooms, worlds or sessions, and are retrieved with keyword search or **hybrid recall**: BM25 text matching fused with vector similarity, relationships, temporal facts, recency and importance. Memory is persistent when you configure a memory store (`ANIMAOS_RS_MEMORY_SQLITE_FILE` or `ANIMAOS_RS_MEMORY_FILE`).

## In This Section

- [Search & Recall](/sdk/memories/recall/) covers keyword search, fused recall, result scoring and recent-memory reads.
- [Evaluation & Retention](/sdk/memories/operations/) covers evaluated writes, evidence tracing, retention, readiness, entities and relationships.
- [Core Memory & Export](/sdk/memories/core/) covers the always-on core blocks, owner edits, temporal facts and downloading memory.

## Create a Memory

```typescript
const memory = await client.memories.create({
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  agentName: 'researcher',
  type: 'fact',
  content: 'Rust daemon memory endpoint created',
  importance: 0.8,
  tags: ['sdk', 'memory'],
  scope: 'shared',
  roomId: 'room-1',
  worldId: 'world-default',
});
```

### `CreateMemoryInput` fields

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `agentId` | `string` | yes | Owning agent identifier |
| `agentName` | `string` | yes | Agent name |
| `type` | `MemoryType` | yes | Memory category |
| `content` | `string` | yes | Memory text |
| `importance` | `number` | yes | Importance score, 0 to 1 |
| `tags` | `string[] \| null` | no | Optional tags |
| `scope` | `MemoryScope` | no | Visibility: `shared`, `private` or `room` |
| `roomId`, `worldId`, `sessionId` | `string` | no | Context the memory belongs to |

`create()` returns the stored `Memory`: `id`, `agentId`, `agentName`, `type`, `content`, `importance`, `createdAt`, optional `tags`, `scope` and optional `roomId`, `worldId`, `sessionId`.

### `MemoryType` values

`fact`, `observation`, `task_result` or `reflection`. The daemon rejects anything else (`type must be one of fact, observation, task_result, reflection`).

### `MemoryScope` values

| Value | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `shared` | Visible to all agents in the same context |
| `private` | Visible only to the owning agent |
| `room` | Visible to agents in the specified room |

<Aside type="note">
  Memories also come from the agent's own tools (`memory_add`, `core_memory`), from conversation and task reviews, and from these routes. There is no per-reply memory evaluator.
</Aside>

## Search Memories

`search()` is keyword search over memory text and filters. Each result is the memory itself with an added `score`: the fields are flat, with no nested `memory` object.

```typescript
const results = await client.memories.search('daemon memory', {
  agentName: 'researcher',
  type: 'fact',
  limit: 5,
  minImportance: 0.5,
});

for (const result of results) {
  console.log(`[${result.score.toFixed(3)}] ${result.content}`);
}
```

### `MemorySearchOptions`

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `agentId`, `agentName` | `string` | Filter by agent |
| `type` | `MemoryType` | Filter by memory type |
| `scope` | `MemoryScope` | Filter by visibility scope |
| `roomId`, `worldId`, `sessionId` | `string` | Filter by context |
| `limit` | `number` | Maximum results |
| `minImportance` | `number` | Minimum importance |

## Recent Memories

```typescript
const memories = await client.memories.recent({
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  scope: 'shared',
  limit: 20,
});
```

`RecentMemoriesOptions` has the same filters as search except `type` and `minImportance`.

## Recall

**Recall** is the richer retrieval API. It returns `{ memory, score, ... }` results ranked by a fusion of:

- lexical matches (BM25)
- vector similarity (semantic embeddings)
- relationship proximity to an entity
- temporal relevance
- recency
- stored importance

```typescript
const results = await client.memories.recall('evidence probe', {
  entityId: 'user-1',
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  temporalLimit: 7,
  limit: 3,
});

for (const r of results) {
  console.log(`score ${r.score.toFixed(3)}: ${r.memory.content}`);
  console.log(`  lexical ${r.lexicalScore.toFixed(3)} vector ${r.vectorScore.toFixed(3)}`);
  console.log(`  relationship ${r.relationshipScore.toFixed(3)} temporal ${r.temporalScore.toFixed(3)}`);
}
```

### `MemoryRecallOptions`

All `MemorySearchOptions` plus:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `entityId` | `string` | Entity for relationship scoring |
| `recallAgentId` | `string` | Agent performing the recall |
| `lexicalLimit` | `number` | Max lexical candidates |
| `recentLimit` | `number` | Max recent candidates |
| `relationshipLimit` | `number` | Max relationship candidates |
| `temporalLimit` | `number` | Temporal window size |

### `MemoryRecallResult`

`memory` (the recalled `Memory`), `score` (fused), and the contributions `lexicalScore`, `vectorScore`, `relationshipScore`, `temporalScore`, `recencyScore`, `importanceScore`.

## Embeddings

The daemon embeds memories in the background. The default is `fastembed` (`intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`, run locally); it starts on hashed vectors, downloads and loads the model, then rebuilds vectors, with keyword search covering memories not yet rebuilt. Other modes (`local`, `ollama`, `openai`, `openai-compatible`, `disabled`) are set with `ANIMAOS_RS_MEMORY_EMBEDDINGS`. Check progress with `client.memories.readiness()` ([Evaluation & Retention](/sdk/memories/operations/#readiness)).

## Evaluate, Retain, Relate

Evaluated writes, evidence traces, retention, readiness, entities and relationships live on [Evaluation & Retention](/sdk/memories/operations/). Editing and deleting individual memories, temporal facts, core memory and export are on [Core Memory & Export](/sdk/memories/core/).
Always-on core memory, owner edits to memories and facts, and downloading an agent's memory

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

These APIs let the owner see and fix what an agent remembers. They are **owner routes**: the daemon refuses them without local-owner authorization (`403 local owner authorization required`). From a script that means sending `Authorization: Bearer <ANIMA_LOCAL_ADMIN_TOKEN>`; see [Authentication](/sdk/client/#authentication). Every response is `Cache-Control: no-store`.

## Core Memory

Each agent has two always-on blocks, shown at the top of every run's context:

| Block | Name in the console | Holds | Budget |
|-------|---------------------|-------|--------|
| `user` | About you | The owner's profile | 1,500 characters |
| `notes` | Agent notes | What the agent learned about its work | 2,500 characters |

An entry is at most 500 characters, and budgets count characters. Entries are stored as private facts tagged `core:user` or `core:notes`, so history, export and scanning apply. Text the threat scanner flags is hidden from the agent and shown as `[entry hidden: flagged <ids>]`. The daemon also keeps read-only `USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` copies under `<workspace>/.animaos-swarm/agent-profiles/`; edits to them are overwritten.

The agent edits core memory with the `core_memory` tool (`add`, `replace` or `remove`). You edit it through the SDK:

```typescript
const core = await client.memories.coreMemory('AGENT_ID');
console.log(core.user.used, '/', core.user.limit, core.user.entries);

const added = await client.memories.addCoreEntry('AGENT_ID', 'user', 'Prefers metric units.');
// added.entryId, added.changed (false for an exact duplicate), added.warnings

await client.memories.updateCoreEntry('AGENT_ID', 'user', added.entryId, 'Prefers metric units and 24-hour time.');
await client.memories.removeCoreEntry('AGENT_ID', 'user', added.entryId);
```

| Method | Returns | Notes |
|--------|---------|-------|
| `coreMemory(agentId, { signal? })` | `CoreMemory` | `{ user, notes }`, each a block with `used`, `limit` and `entries` (`id`, `content`, `flagged`) |
| `addCoreEntry(agentId, block, text)` | `CoreMemoryEdit` | Both blocks as they are now, plus `entryId`, `changed` and `warnings` |
| `updateCoreEntry(agentId, block, entryId, text)` | `CoreMemoryEdit` | Same shape |
| `removeCoreEntry(agentId, block, entryId)` | `CoreMemoryEdit` | Same shape |

Entry text is untrusted (the agent may have written it): show it as text, not markup. Flagged text you save is stored anyway and reported in `warnings`. Generic memory routes refuse to edit a core entry or add a core tag.

Conversation reviews, which run every 10 owner messages and may propose core-memory edits, are covered in [MCP, Skills & Learning](/sdk/extensions/#learning-reviews).

## Edit and Delete Memories

```typescript
const edited = await client.memories.update('MEMORY_ID', {
  content: 'Corrected text',
  importance: 0.9,
  tags: null, // null clears the tags; omit to keep them; an array replaces them
});

const removed = await client.memories.delete('MEMORY_ID', 'Corrected text');
console.log(removed.removedRelationships, removed.updatedFacts);
```

- `update()` patches `content`, `importance` and `tags`, and the content is re-indexed and re-embedded. The SDK exports the daemon's limits as constants: `MAX_MEMORY_EDIT_CHARS` (8,000), `MAX_MEMORY_TAGS` (20) and `MAX_MEMORY_TAG_CHARS` (40).
- `delete(id, expectedContent?)` removes the memory and drops it from fact and relationship citations. With `expectedContent`, the daemon checks the exact current text under its write lock and answers `409` if it changed; without it, the older id-only deletion applies. It returns `{ id, removedRelationships, updatedRelationships, updatedFacts }`.

## Temporal Facts

Temporal facts record a subject, predicate, value and validity window, with the memories that evidence them. They carry no agent of their own: an agent's facts are those whose evidence includes one of its memories.

```typescript
const facts = await client.memories.facts({ agentId: 'AGENT_ID', subject: 'user-42', limit: 50 });

const { fact, superseded } = await client.memories.replaceFact(facts[0].id, 'New value');
await client.memories.deleteFact(fact.id);
```

- `facts({ agentId, subject, includeInactive, limit })` lists newest first. `limit` is 1 to 500 (default 100); `subject` matches the subject id, or the subject name ignoring ASCII case; `includeInactive: true` adds superseded and retracted facts (`status` is `active`, `superseded` or `retracted`).
- `replaceFact(factId, value)` (1 to `MAX_FACT_VALUE_CHARS`, 500, characters) saves a new active fact that supersedes the old one. Only an active fact with a value can be edited (`409` otherwise).
- `deleteFact(factId)` returns `{ id }`.
- `deleteEntity(kind, entityId)` removes an entity plus the relationships and facts that name it, and answers `409` while the entity still has memories. Deleting the `user` entity is soft in practice: a later relationship or fact that names the user recreates it.

Fact and entity text is untrusted; display it as text.

## Export

```typescript
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const blob = await client.memories.exportMemories({ format: 'md', agentId: 'AGENT_ID' });
await writeFile('anima-memory.md', Buffer.from(await blob.arrayBuffer()));
```

`exportMemories({ format?, agentId? })` returns a `Blob`: `json` (the default) or `md`, for one agent or, without `agentId`, every agent. Embedding vectors are never exported.

The JSON document has `version`, `exportedAt` and an `agents` array. Each agent entry holds `id`, `name`, `core` (`user` and `notes` entries), its `memories` (newest first, core entries excluded), `entities`, `relationships` and `temporalFacts`. An all-agents export adds `unattributed` with the entities, relationships and facts no agent section holds, so nothing is left out. The Markdown export groups memories by type.

<Aside type="note">
  Export, edits and deletes act on the daemon's store only. Old chats, receipts and backups may still contain removed text.
</Aside>

## Evaluate Before Writing

```typescript
const evaluation = await client.memories.evaluate({
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  agentName: 'researcher',
  type: 'fact',
  content: 'Something happened',
  importance: 0.5,
});

console.log(evaluation.decision, evaluation.reason, evaluation.score);
```

`evaluate()` takes the same fields as `create()` plus optional `minContentChars` and `minImportance`, and stores nothing. It returns a `MemoryEvaluation`: `decision` (`store`, `merge` or `ignore`), `reason`, `score`, `suggestedImportance` and `duplicateMemoryId` for a merge.

## Evaluate and Store

```typescript
const outcome = await client.memories.addEvaluated({
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  agentName: 'researcher',
  type: 'fact',
  content: 'User prefers concise release notes',
  importance: 0.4,
  tags: ['preference'],
  minContentChars: 8,
  minImportance: 0.1,
});

console.log(outcome.evaluation.decision, outcome.memory?.id);
```

The outcome holds the `evaluation` and the stored `memory`, which is `null` unless the decision was `store`; duplicate or low-value candidates add no new record.

## Evidence Trace

```typescript
const trace = await client.memories.trace('MEMORY_ID');

console.log(trace.memory.content);
console.log(trace.relationships.length, trace.entities.length);
```

The trace returns the memory, the relationships that cite it and the entities involved. Use it when the app needs to explain why a memory matters.

## Retention and Cleanup

```typescript
const report = await client.memories.applyRetention({
  minImportance: 0.2,
  maxMemories: 1000,
  maxAgeMillis: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  decayHalfLifeMillis: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
});

console.log(report.decayedMemories.length, report.removedMemoryIds.length);
```

All four fields are optional.

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `maxAgeMillis` | Remove memories older than this |
| `minImportance` | Remove memories below this importance |
| `maxMemories` | Keep at most this many |
| `decayHalfLifeMillis` | Half-life for importance decay |

The report has `decayedMemories` (`memoryId`, `previousImportance`, `newImportance`), `removedMemoryIds` and `removedRelationshipIds`.

## Readiness

```typescript
const ready = await client.memories.readiness();

console.log(ready.passed, ready.embeddings.vectorCount);
console.log(ready.embeddings.status, ready.embeddings.done, ready.embeddings.total);
console.log(ready.externalProvider?.status);
console.log(ready.evaluation.passedChecks, '/', ready.evaluation.totalChecks);
```

### `MemoryReadiness`

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `passed` | `boolean` | Overall status |
| `embeddings` | `MemoryEmbeddingStatus` | Embedding engine status |
| `externalProvider` | `ExternalMemoryProviderStatus` (optional) | The external memory provider beside the local store (`none` by default); absent from older daemons |
| `evaluation` | `MemoryEvalReport` | Baseline eval harness result: `passed`, `totalChecks`, `passedChecks`, `failureMessages`, `cases` |

### `MemoryEmbeddingStatus`

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `enabled` | `boolean` | Whether embeddings are active |
| `provider`, `model` | `string` | Embedding provider and model |
| `dimension` | `number` | Vector size |
| `vectorCount` | `number` | Vectors stored |
| `persisted` | `boolean` | Whether vectors are persisted |
| `storageFile` | `string \| null` | Vector store file, when any |
| `status` | `MemoryEmbeddingLoadStatus` | `downloading`, `rebuilding`, `ready`, `fallback` or `off`; the search model loads in the background after boot |
| `done`, `total` | `number` | Memories with a vector from the active embedder, out of those to embed (`rebuilding` shows progress) |
| `reason` | `string` (optional) | Why search fell back to basic search; only with `fallback` |

`ExternalMemoryProviderStatus` is `{ id, status: 'ready' | 'unavailable', reason? }`. Only `none` is built in today.

## Entities and Relationships

Entities and relationships form an explicit graph that recall uses for relationship scoring.

```typescript
const entity = await client.memories.createEntity({
  kind: 'user',
  id: 'user-42',
  name: 'Alice',
  aliases: ['al', 'ali'],
  summary: 'A power user who prefers CLI tools.',
});

const relationship = await client.memories.createRelationship({
  sourceKind: 'agent',
  sourceAgentId: 'agent-a',
  sourceAgentName: 'researcher',
  targetKind: 'agent',
  targetAgentId: 'agent-b',
  targetAgentName: 'writer',
  relationshipType: 'collaborator',
  strength: 0.9,
  confidence: 0.85,
});

const entities = await client.memories.entities({ kind: 'user', limit: 50 });
const relationships = await client.memories.relationships({
  agentId: 'agent-a',
  relationshipType: 'collaborator',
  minStrength: 0.5,
  limit: 10,
});

console.log(entity.id, relationship.relationshipType, entities.length, relationships.length);
```

`createEntity` and `createRelationship` create or update. Entity `kind` and relationship `sourceKind` and `targetKind` are one of `agent`, `user`, `system` or `external` (relationship kinds default to `agent`).

### `NewAgentRelationshipInput`

Required: `sourceAgentId`, `sourceAgentName`, `targetAgentId`, `targetAgentName`, `relationshipType`. Optional: `sourceKind`, `targetKind`, `summary`, `strength`, `confidence`, `evidenceMemoryIds`, `tags`, `roomId`, `worldId`, `sessionId`.

### `AgentRelationshipOptions`

Filters for `relationships()`: `agentId`, `entityId`, `sourceKind`, `sourceAgentId`, `targetKind`, `targetAgentId`, `relationshipType`, `roomId`, `worldId`, `sessionId`, `minStrength`, `minConfidence`, `limit`.

### `MemoryEntity`

`kind`, `id`, `name`, `aliases`, `summary` (`string | null`), `createdAt`, `updatedAt`. `entities()` filters by `entityId`, `kind`, `name`, `alias` and `limit`.

Keyword search, fused recall, recent-memory reads, and score interpretation in the SDK

import { Aside, Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Memory retrieval has three levels:

- `search()` for keyword lookup with filters
- `recall()` for fused ranking across lexical, vector, relationship, temporal, recency and importance signals
- `recent()` for freshness

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="Search">
    Use `search()` for direct keyword or filter-driven lookup. Results are flat memories with a `score`.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Recall">
    Use `recall()` when you want a fused ranking with per-signal scores. Results nest the memory under `memory`.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Recent">
    Use `recent()` when freshness matters more than retrieval scoring.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

## Search

```typescript
const results = await client.memories.search('daemon memory', {
  agentName: 'researcher',
  type: 'fact',
  limit: 5,
  minImportance: 0.5,
});

for (const result of results) {
  console.log(result.score, result.content, result.tags);
}
```

`MemorySearchResult` is a `Memory` plus `score`, so read `result.content`, not `result.memory.content`. The daemon also serves the same search at `GET /api/search`.

## Recent Memories

```typescript
const memories = await client.memories.recent({
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  scope: 'shared',
  limit: 20,
});
```

For one agent's most recent memories without other filters, `client.agents.recentMemories(agentId, { limit })` is also available.

## Fused Recall

```typescript
const results = await client.memories.recall('evidence probe', {
  entityId: 'user-1',
  agentId: 'AGENT_ID',
  temporalLimit: 7,
  limit: 3,
});

for (const r of results) {
  console.log(r.score, r.memory.content);
  console.log(r.lexicalScore, r.vectorScore, r.relationshipScore);
}
```

## How to Read Recall Scores

Recall combines:

- lexical match (BM25)
- vector similarity from the configured embedder
- relationship proximity to `entityId`
- temporal relevance
- recency
- stored importance

You do not need the weighting math. What matters is that recall is intentionally richer than search: each result exposes `lexicalScore`, `vectorScore`, `relationshipScore`, `temporalScore`, `recencyScore` and `importanceScore` next to the fused `score`, so you can see why a memory surfaced.

<Aside type="note">
  Vector scores depend on the embedder. The default `fastembed` model loads in the background after startup; until it is ready (or if it fails to load), the daemon uses hashed vectors and keyword search. `client.memories.readiness()` reports the state.
</Aside>

<Aside type="tip">
  Reach for `search()` when you already know what you are looking for. Reach for `recall()` when the system should infer the best supporting memories from several signals.
</Aside>

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The SDK is one `DaemonClient` with typed sub-clients, plus shared types. It is a client for the [Rust daemon](https://github.com/G9000/animaOS-SWARM/tree/main/hosts/rust-daemon) over HTTP and SSE; the daemon's own route inventory and OpenAPI document (`GET /openapi.json`, browsable at `/docs`) are the contract behind it. Methods marked **owner** use owner routes and need `Authorization: Bearer <ANIMA_LOCAL_ADMIN_TOKEN>` from a script ([Authentication](/sdk/client/#authentication)).

All `signal` options are an `AbortSignal`. Unless noted, methods resolve to the unwrapped payload (for example `agents.get()` returns the `AgentSnapshot`, not `{ agent }`).

## `DaemonClient`

```typescript
import { createDaemonClient, DaemonClient } from '@animaOS-SWARM/sdk';

const client = createDaemonClient(options);
```

| `DaemonClientOptions` | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------------------|------|---------|-------------|
| `baseUrl` | `string` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080` | Daemon origin or path prefix; `''` for same-origin browsers |
| `fetch` | `FetchLike` | `globalThis.fetch` | Custom fetch (add auth headers here) |

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `health()` | `GET /health`: `{ status: 'ok' }` |
| `capabilities()` | `GET /api/capabilities`: `DaemonCapabilities` |
| `requestJson<T>(path, init?)` | JSON request; objects in `body` are serialized, `FormData`, `Blob` and strings pass through |
| `requestText(path, init?)` | Text response (Markdown, CSV) |
| `requestBlob(path, init?)` | Binary response |
| `requestBoundedBlob(path, init, limits)` | Binary response with a strict size and content-type check |
| `requestNoBody(path, init, expectedStatus)` | Status-only call; the body is discarded |
| `subscribe<T>(path, init?)` | Async generator of `DaemonEvent<T>` (`event`, `data`, optional `id`) over SSE |

Sub-clients: `agents`, `swarms`, `memories`, `sessions`, `runs`, `events`, `attachments`, `approvals`, `automations`, `goals`, `mcp`, `skills`, `communityBundles`, `learning`, `usage`, `logs`, `status`, `system`, `workspace`, `agentFiles`, `agencies`, `connectors`, `voice`, `speech`, `browserScopes`, `chatgpt`.

### Errors

| Class | Thrown when | Properties |
|-------|-------------|------------|
| `DaemonHttpError` | Non-2xx response | `status`, `body` |
| `DaemonConnectionError` | The daemon cannot be reached or the body fails midway | `cause` |
| `DaemonTooOldError` | `sessions.list()` or `sessions.main()` on a daemon without sessions | `code: 'daemon_too_old'`, `agentId` |
| `StatusTooOldError` | `status.get()` on a daemon without `/api/status` | `code: 'daemon_too_old'` |

## `AgentsClient` (`client.agents`)

See [Agents](/sdk/agents/).

| Method | Returns | Description |
